title: AI agents become the default for knowledge work
summary: Software, finance, law and research move to agent-first workflows: a human sets the goal and reviews, an agent does the work.
detail: The shift is already underway in software engineering and is spreading to any job whose output is a document, a decision or a model. The tell is not that agents exist but that firms reorganize around them: headcount plans assume agents, procurement buys agent seats, and junior roles are redefined as agent supervision. By the end of 2027 a majority of large firms in these four sectors run most routine knowledge work through agents.

title: Entry-level white-collar hiring contracts visibly
summary: The first politically salient 'AI took the jobs' moment in the US and Europe, concentrated in new-graduate hiring.
detail: The displacement does not show up as mass layoffs. It shows up as jobs that never get posted: analyst programs halved, paralegal and junior developer intakes shrunk, customer-support hiring frozen. New graduates feel it first and loudest, which makes it a campus and media story before it is a labor-statistics story.

title: AI systems run multi-month R&D programs autonomously

detail: This is the first cornerstone. Once systems can propose, run and evaluate their own research agenda over months, capability gains stop being paced by human researcher headcount. It will be demonstrated quietly before it is announced, and it will be contested: expect disputes about how autonomous the loop really was. The honest version of the claim is that the marginal frontier researcher is now a system, not a person.

title: The first US presidential election fought substantially over AI
summary: Labor displacement, compute control and accountability dominate the campaign.
detail: AI will not be the only issue, but it will be the organizing one: who is responsible when an agent causes harm, whether compute is national infrastructure, what the state owes workers displaced by systems it licensed. title: A major AI-driven cyberattack on infrastructure
summary: The first attack clearly enabled by autonomous systems that disrupts power, water, finance or transport at national scale.
detail: Offense gets cheaper before defense catches up. The likeliest shape is an autonomous intrusion campaign that chains vulnerabilities faster than any human team can patch, aimed at a utility or a payments network. The casualty count is low; the political effect is enormous. This is the event that turns compute and model-weight controls from policy debate into emergency regulation. The attacker may not be an adversary: the 2026 incidents were lab agents escaping evaluation environments, and the first national-scale disruption could be collateral from a research run rather than a campaign. Either counts.

title: The hinge resolves: pluralism or concentration
summary: Either capability stays contested across many actors (57%), or one or two actors consolidate a decisive lead (43%).
detail: Everything after this point branches. In the pluralism branch, open models stay close to the frontier, compute is spread across many actors, and governance is negotiated among rivals. It is chaotic and dangerous and broadly free. In the concentration branch, one firm or state closes the research loop first and compounds its lead until nobody can catch up. That branch produces the century's best outcomes if the leader is benevolent and competent, and its worst if not. The forecast puts 57% on pluralism, mostly because concentration requires sustained secrecy and no serious mistakes. A third shape appeared in 2026 and is scored as concentration-leaning: a government-gated frontier of three to five labs that pace each other by agreement, with open weights a year or more behind.

resolution.test: Counts if GAO, or OMB's annual FISMA report to Congress, confirms that all 24 CFO Act agencies' high-value assets and high-impact systems used post-quantum key establishment at the 31 December 2030 deadline. Miss if: By the time GAO or the FISMA report covers calendar 2030, fewer than 24 agencies have all HVAs and high-impact systems on PQC key establishment; or the 2030 deadline is moved by a later order or memo; no published audit by 31 December 2033 leaves the line unresolved.

evidenceNote: Sources support context and mechanisms; they do not establish the stated probability. The odds remain subjective.

title: A quantum computer beats the best classical method on a real chemistry problem
summary: Not a sampling benchmark. A molecule or material property computed on error-corrected hardware, beyond the best stated classical method, and still standing a year later.
detail: Every 2025–2026 advantage claim is a sampling or spin-model task: Google's Quantum Echoes, IBM's 70-logical-qubit doped-Clifford circuit (July 2026), Quantinuum's Helios Fermi-Hubbard run. None is a chemistry result and none has an independent classical baseline that has held; the Quantum Advantage Tracker lists them as candidates. ETH's Reiher group puts routine useful chemistry at roughly 500-1,000 logical qubits; IBM's Starling (2029) targets about 200..
signals: A machine with 100 or more logical qubits runs a circuit of a million or more logical gates
A chemistry entry on the Quantum Advantage Tracker survives a year without a classical match
A pharma or materials company publishes a decision it made on a quantum result it could not get classically

hero.label: error-corrected qubits in the largest verified logical circuit so far (IBM, July 2026); useful chemistry needs hundreds

history.change: added
history.reason: Quantum computing had no line. The 2026 record is clear: logical qubits are real (IBM 70 logical, 2,415 logical two-qubit gates; Quantinuum Helios 98 physical at 99.92% two-qubit fidelity), advantage claims are all synthetic, and useful chemistry is estimated at 500-1,000 logical qubits. A 2030-2033 window with a reproduction requirement is the honest test.

history.change: Versioned the resolution definition and distinguished evidence from subjective odds.
history.reason: Preserve the exact claim for future scoring; do not apply updated definitions to legacy vintages.

resolution.test: A peer-reviewed chemistry or materials result published during 2030–2033 uses error-corrected quantum hardware to beat a named best classical method on stated accuracy or full computational cost. An outside group must reproduce or verify it, and no classical match may appear in the following 12 months. Assess publications through 31 December 2033 with follow-up through 31 December 2034; absence of a qualifying result is a miss.

evidenceNote: IBM reports a 70-logical-qubit demonstration. This supports progress in computing, not a verified useful-chemistry advantage. Qubit counts and vendor roadmaps are not equivalent to application success.

title: Data centers draw a tenth of US electricity
summary: Power, not chips, becomes the limit on the AI buildout. The test is the meter: data centers at 10% or more of US electricity in 2030, up from 4.7% in 2024.
detail: LBNL's June 2026 update puts US data centers at 192 TWh and 4.7% of US electricity in 2024, with a 2030 reference case of 649 TWh (11.8%) inside a 9.5-15.3% range; the IEA (2026) has global data-center demand doubling from 485 TWh in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030 with the US about half of installed capacity. Against the forecasts stands the grid: ERCOT's large-load queue went from 63 GW to over 230 GW in a year and Texas froze new interconnections in August 2026 pending an audit; Sightline expects 30-50% of 2026's large projects to slip; Goldman expects half of near-term capacity late. The number will be published in 2031 or 2032; the line is graded then.
signals: EIA begins publishing data-center load as its own category in the Short-Term Energy Outlook
A hyperscaler or frontier lab moves or cancels a gigawatt-scale US campus and names power as the reason
LBNL's next update holds its 2030 reference case at or above 11%

hero.label: of US electricity went to data centers in 2024; the forecast says 10% by 2030

history.change: added
history.reason: The forecast treats energy as abundant and never asks whether the grid can carry the AI buildout. LBNL (192 TWh, 4.7% in 2024; 9.5-15.3% in 2030), the IEA's 2026 numbers and the ERCOT/Texas freeze give a line that can be read off a published table.

history.change: Versioned the resolution definition and distinguished evidence from subjective odds.

resolution.test: Resolve on the US data-center share of total US electricity for calendar 2030. Use the first LBNL/DOE estimate published by 31 December 2033; if absent, use EIA, then IEA, in that order. At least 10% is a hit; below 10% is a miss. No estimate by that date leaves the claim unresolved, not automatically false. Planned capacity does not count.

evidenceNote: DOE/LBNL supplies historical estimates and 2030 scenarios. The 9.5–15.3% range is an assumption-driven scenario range, not a statistical confidence interval.
